text: The company decided to invest in new technology. ___ proved to be a very wise decision.
explanation: 'This' refers back to the entire previous sentence (the decision to invest), bringing the idea into the present discussion.

text: I really enjoyed the books you lent me, especially the ___ about ancient history.
explanation: 'ones' substitutes for the plural countable noun 'books'.

text: Mary didn't finish the assignment on time, but I ___.
explanation: We use the auxiliary 'did' to avoid repeating the main verb 'finish'.

text: He asked me if the train was delayed, and I told him I hoped ___.
explanation: After 'hope', we use 'not' to substitute a negative clause (I hoped it was not delayed).

text: I would love to travel to Japan next year. I really hope ___.
explanation: 'so' substitutes the affirmative clause after 'hope'.

text: Are you going to the concert tonight? If ___, we could share a taxi.
explanation: 'If so' replaces the entire conditional clause 'If you are going to the concert tonight'.

text: I have never been scuba diving before, but my brother ___.
explanation: The auxiliary 'has' is used to avoid repeating 'been scuba diving'.

text: She promised to help me with the project, but she didn't want ___.
explanation: The infinitive 'to' is left alone, omitting the rest of the clause (to help me).

text: The manager resigned suddenly, and nobody understands ___.
explanation: The wh-word 'why' is left alone to omit 'why he resigned'.

text: Some people believe that the economy will recover soon. ___ experts, however, disagree.
explanation: 'These' refers to the experts related to the current topic of discussion.

text: I ordered a coffee and ___ sat down at the table.
explanation: We can omit the subject after 'and' if it is the same as the first clause.

text: He refused to apologize, and ___ made the situation even worse.
explanation: 'That' refers back to the entire previous action (refusing to apologize) as a completed past event.

text: I don't think we should buy a new car. Neither ___ my wife.
explanation: 'Neither + aux + subject' is used to agree with a negative statement.

text: We need to submit the report by Friday. If ___, we will lose the contract.
explanation: 'If not' replaces the negative conditional clause 'If we do not submit the report by Friday'.

text: The students who passed the exam were the ___ who studied regularly.
explanation: 'ones' replaces the plural noun 'students'.

text: I thought the meeting was going to be cancelled, but it ___.
explanation: The auxiliary 'wasn't' avoids repeating 'cancelled'.

text: Would you like to come to the cinema with us? I'd love ___.
explanation: The infinitive particle 'to' is left alone, omitting 'come to the cinema'.

text: I'm not sure if the store is open on Sundays, but I suppose ___.
explanation: After 'suppose', we use 'so' to substitute the affirmative clause.

text: They promised to clean the house, and they ___.
explanation: 'did so' replaces the verb + object 'cleaned the house'.

text: I used to play tennis a lot, but I haven't ___ for years.
explanation: 'done so' substitutes the verb and its object 'played tennis'.

text: She was wearing a beautiful dress, the ___ I bought for her birthday.
explanation: 'one' substitutes the singular countable noun 'dress'.

text: Will the new policy affect our department? I expect ___.
explanation: 'not' is used after 'expect' to replace a negative clause.

text: He bought a new laptop and ___ a printer.
explanation: We can omit the verb 'bought' because it is understood from the first clause.

text: She has been working here for ten years. ___ is why she knows everything.
explanation: 'That' refers back to the fact mentioned in the previous sentence.

text: I really enjoy reading science fiction novels. So ___ my best friend.
explanation: 'So + auxiliary + subject' for agreement. The auxiliary 'does' matches the present simple tense of 'enjoy'.

text: The cake ___ I baked yesterday was delicious.
explanation: We can omit the relative pronoun 'that/which' when it acts as the object of the relative clause.

text: I told him to finish the report, but he didn't want ___.
explanation: We leave the 'to' to omit the rest of the infinitive clause.

text: Someone left the door open, but I don't know ___.
explanation: The wh-word 'who' stands alone, omitting 'left the door open'.

text: We need more volunteers for the event. Are you available? If ___, please sign up here.
explanation: 'If so' replaces 'If you are available'.

text: My old phone was broken, so I had to buy a new ___.
explanation: 'one' substitutes the singular noun 'phone'.
